Getting Started: RNA-Seq Mixed Model Pipeline

Source: vignettes/rnaseq-nb-pipeline.Rmd
rnaseq-nb-pipeline.Rmd

Why not just fit each gene separately?

The traditional approach to RNA-seq differential expression – a separate negative binomial GLM per gene – treats every gene as if it told you nothing about any other gene. fit_rnaseq_nb_pipeline() instead fits one multilevel model across all genes at once, with a gene-level random slope for the effect of interest. Genes with little data (or noisy counts) get pulled (“shrunk”) toward the population-average effect; genes with strong, consistent evidence keep their own estimate. This is the same partial-pooling idea behind lme4/brms random effects, applied to differential expression.

Note on this vignette: the code chunks below are shown but not evaluated during package build (eval = FALSE), because fitting even a small Stan model takes longer than is reasonable for a vignette build step, and brms is a Suggests dependency precisely so omicsuite doesn’t force a Stan toolchain on everyone who only wants the survival module. Copy these chunks into an interactive session to run them for real.

library(omicsuite)
library(brms)

A simulated example 

set.seed(1)
n_genes <- 20
n_samples <- 16

dat <- expand.grid(
  gene   = paste0("gene_", seq_len(n_genes)),
  sample = paste0("sample_", seq_len(n_samples)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
dat$condition <- factor(rep(
  rep(c("control", "treated"), each = n_samples / 2), n_genes
))
# a handful of genes get a real treatment effect; the rest are noise
responsive_genes <- paste0("gene_", 1:4)
dat$mu <- ifelse(
  dat$gene %in% responsive_genes & dat$condition == "treated",
  80, 40
)
dat$count <- stats::rnbinom(nrow(dat), mu = dat$mu, size = 4)

fit <- fit_rnaseq_nb_pipeline(
  data          = dat,
  gene_var      = "gene",
  count_var     = "count",
  condition_var = "condition",
  sample_var    = "sample",
  chains = 4, iter = 2000, warmup = 1000,
  cache_file = "rnaseq_vignette_fit.rds"
)

fit

Reading the output 

fit$verdicts

mcmc_convergence is the one to check before trusting anything else – if Rhat is elevated or the effective-sample-size ratio is low, more iterations (or a reparameterized model) come before any biological interpretation. dispersion[shape] is informational: a large shape parameter means the negative binomial is behaving close to Poisson for this dataset. posterior_predictive_check is a visual check, not an automatic pass/fail – see the plot below.

plot(fit, which = "pp_check")
plot(fit, which = "rhat_plot")

The shrinkage plot

This is the plot that makes the partial-pooling worth it: each gene’s condition effect, shrunk toward the population-level estimate (dashed line) in proportion to how much evidence that gene provides.

plot(fit, which = "shrinkage_plot")
head(fit$shrinkage[order(-abs(fit$shrinkage$gene_deviation)), ])

The genes furthest from the dashed line in the plot – and at the top of this sorted table – are the ones with the strongest evidence of a condition-specific effect after accounting for what every other gene in the dataset is doing.
